lines: Telo Ride gets a backend, kept thin: only what one browser cannot do alone. It never talks to the bike.
Four projects: domain, application, infrastructure and the API.
Each references only the layer before it, so the compiler holds the direction.
Every request takes one path. A controller checks nothing: it sends one MediatR request, its validators run, then its handler.
Two health endpoints answer without a session. Live says the API responds.
Ready says Unhealthy, with a 503, while the database cannot be reached.
Every other address needs a signed-in rider. Without a session, the answer is 401, as ProblemDetails, never a redirect.
Every refusal carries a code a screen can branch on: validation failed, a domain rule like session full, or unexpected, which reveals nothing.
Telemetry is OpenTelemetry, with Telo Ride's own counter on the Telo Ride meter.
A span names its route by template, never the query string.
The schema changes only through migrations, applied by the migrate command before a new version starts. The API never migrates on start-up.
Riders see nothing new yet. The app still rides on its own, on a phone, a tablet, a laptop or a desktop.
What the tests prove: sixteen acceptance tests through the API, on a real host in memory, with no real database, no file and no sleep.
Telo Ride, from the Telo family, turns a smart bike at home into a game.
It pairs with the bike over Bluetooth, reads your power and sets resistance for every hill and interval.

lines.text: Two doors: Race, ride a map against your best-time ghost, bots or people; and Classes, ride along to a video, alone or with a group; fed by one progression of XP, rider levels, stars and map unlocks.
